reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Corneal dystrophies are inherited, usually bilateral and symmetrical, non-inflammatory disorders that progress slowly and are typically classified by the corneal layer chiefly affected
Anterior (epithelial and Bowman) dystrophies such as epithelial basement membrane dystrophy often cause recurrent corneal erosions with episodic pain, tearing, and morning symptoms
Stromal dystrophies (lattice, granular, macular) deposit characteristic material and progressively reduce clarity and vision
Fuchs endothelial dystrophy causes progressive endothelial cell loss, corneal guttata, and stromal oedema that leads to worse vision on waking that improves through the day
Slit-lamp examination and family history are central to diagnosis, and the pattern of deposits helps identify the subtype
Specular or confocal microscopy and corneal pachymetry help assess endothelial function and corneal thickness in endothelial disease
Management ranges from lubricants and hypertonic agents for symptomatic relief to phototherapeutic keratectomy for anterior disease and lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for advanced visual loss
Some stromal dystrophies can recur in a corneal graft, which is relevant when planning surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Corneal dystrophies are genetically determined disorders in which abnormal material accumulates within, or normal cells are progressively lost from, a specific corneal layer. Many stromal dystrophies (lattice, granular, and the related TGFBI group) result from mutations causing deposition of amyloid or hyaline material that scatters light. Macular dystrophy reflects a defect in keratan sulphate metabolism with mucopolysaccharide deposition. In Fuchs endothelial dystrophy the endothelial pump fails as cells are lost and guttata form, so the stroma imbibes fluid and swells, producing oedema and, in advanced cases, epithelial bullae. Anterior dystrophies disrupt epithelial adhesion, predisposing to recurrent erosions.
additionalDifferentials: Corneal degenerations such as band keratopathy or Salzmann nodular degeneration
Corneal deposits from systemic or drug causes
Recurrent erosion from prior corneal trauma
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to define the affected layer and deposit pattern
Corneal pachymetry to quantify thickness and oedema in endothelial disease
Specular or confocal microscopy to assess endothelial cell density and guttata
Corneal topography or tomography to exclude ectasia and plan surgery
Family history and, where available, genetic testing to confirm the subtype
redFlags: Sudden pain and redness suggesting a ruptured epithelial bulla or secondary microbial keratitis rather than the dystrophy itself
Rapid loss of vision that is out of keeping with a slowly progressive dystrophy
Corneal decompensation after intraocular surgery in an eye with borderline endothelial function
Graft failure or dystrophy recurrence after keratoplasty
reference.prognosis: Most dystrophies progress slowly over years; anterior disease is often controlled with conservative measures, while advanced stromal opacity or endothelial decompensation may require keratoplasty, which restores useful vision in many cases although some stromal dystrophies can recur in the graft.
pitfalls: Mistaking a bilateral inherited dystrophy for a unilateral infective or degenerative process
Treating recurrent erosions symptomatically without recognising an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy
Proceeding to cataract surgery without assessing endothelial reserve in suspected Fuchs dystrophy
Overlooking the risk of dystrophy recurrence when counselling about corneal grafting
management: Manage anterior dystrophies and recurrent erosions conservatively with ocular lubricants, hypertonic saline ointment and bandage contact lenses, escalating to epithelial debridement or phototherapeutic keratectomy
Reduce stromal oedema in endothelial disease with topical hypertonic saline and treat bullous keratopathy symptomatically
Offer endothelial keratoplasty for endothelial decompensation and lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for visually significant stromal opacity
Monitor progression with slit-lamp biomicroscopy, corneal pachymetry and specular or confocal microscopy of endothelial function
Provide genetic counselling and, where available, confirmatory genetic testing for these inherited disorders
Arrange ophthalmology follow-up with graft surveillance, recognising that some stromal dystrophies can recur in a transplant
Refer to a corneal specialist for surgical planning and management of complications
